clue.text: Famed judge imposing fines in Channel island, with son the latest

indicators.note: son becomes the latest, so its letter shifts from its place to the very end
the fines are imposed, set down, within the island's name
the fines go in the island, so the island's name is the container

parts.note: Jersey is one of the Channel Islands
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine, so two of them make FF

explanation.surface: A notorious judge is pictured slapping fines on Jersey residents, his son following in his footsteps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fines' as two F's is the pencil-grading convention; 'the latest' means the son's letter is moved to the very end rather than added.
explanation.definitionFit: George Jeffreys was the infamous 'hanging judge' of the Bloody Assizes after Monmouth's rebellion in 1685.

clue.text: Close to catastrophe, aeroplane screens primarily command this?

definitions.text: Close to catastrophe, aeroplane screens primarily command this?

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter
the aircraft screens, shields, a letter inside its name
primarily means first, so take the opening letter

explanation.surface: With disaster looming, a plane's screens flash the order to bail out.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: near catastrophe, the order a pilot's screens would give is to leave the aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: To eject is to fire oneself out of a stricken aircraft by ejector seat, the command given in an emergency.

clue.text: Lush facilities embraced by rowing team?

indicators.note: the facilities are held within the team's name

parts.note: a four, or foursome, is a rowing crew of four oarsmen
lav, short for lavatory, is the facilities

explanation.surface: A rowing crew enjoys luxurious amenities on their boathouse premises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lush' looks like an adjective about plush facilities, but here it means tasty.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang lush means delicious, which is what a flavoursome dish is.

clue.text: Boxer's in middle of frequent match

indicators.note: the boxer's name goes inside the middle letters
only the middle of the word is kept, its outer pairs of letters trimmed off

parts.note: taken as written before the trim
Ali, the boxer Muhammad Ali, plus the 's

explanation.surface: A boxer appears in the heart of a regular bout.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle is four letters here, not the usual one or two; the boxer's name then sits just before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To equalise is to make level, to match the opponent's score.

clue.text: Rising American bod in charge flourishes, creating shock waves

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means read from the bottom up

parts.note: a bod is a person, in British slang

explanation.surface: An upwardly mobile American manager thrives, sending shock waves through the business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' reverses US to SU in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonic booms are the pressure waves heard when aircraft exceed the speed of sound.

clue.text: New question on supermarket's financial data system

indicators.note: in an across entry, on means placed after, so the question follows the supermarket

parts.note: Asda is a British supermarket chain

explanation.surface: A new query about a supermarket's financial records.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts the question after the supermarket in the across entry; Asda is a large UK supermarket chain.
explanation.definitionFit: NASDAQ is the American electronic stock exchange, originally an automated quotation system.

clue.text: Thought, on the way up, PC World opens midday

indicators.note: the reversed letters open up noon, sitting in its middle
in a down entry, going up means the letters are read backwards

parts.note: IT, information technology, is the world of PCs

explanation.surface: A shopper muses that the PC World store opens at noon.
explanation.walkthrough: PC World is a British computer retailer, which hides its real job: the world of PCs is information technology.
explanation.definitionFit: A notion is an idea or belief held in the mind.

clue.text: Stray spades wearing

parts.note: S is the card-suit abbreviation for spades

explanation.surface: A card game where a stray spade is being worn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stray' is the verb, to go astray morally.
explanation.definitionFit: To sin is to stray from the right path, a moral lapse.

clue.text: Bitter maybe about Barney discarding central watercolour painting

indicators.note: the ale goes around the other part

parts.note: bitter is a kind of ale

indicators.note: the central letter of the seven-letter word is dropped

parts.note: a barney is British slang for a quarrel

explanation.surface: A beer drinker drops a central part of a pub argument over a watercolour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barney' looks like a name but is British slang for a row; with seven letters its centre is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquarelle is a painting technique using transparent washes of watercolour.

clue.text: Jade, shaking light, brought about illusion

indicators.note: the letters of jade are shaken into a new order
brought about means turned around, so the letters run backwards

explanation.surface: Jade, shaking in the light, causes an illusion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' is ultraviolet, abbreviated; 'brought about' turns it round rather than meaning caused.
explanation.definitionFit: Déjà vu is the illusory feeling of having already experienced the present moment.

clue.text: Jerks with armoured vehicle caught game

parts.note: physical jerks are PE, physical education exercises

indicators.note: caught as in heard, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a tank is an armoured vehicle

explanation.surface: Fitness exercises in a tank are an odd sort of game.
explanation.walkthrough: The French ending -anque is said much like 'tank'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pétanque is the French bowls game played with metal balls on gravel.

clue.text: Dry piercing wheels needing oil

indicators.note: the dry letters pierce, go inside, the wheels

parts.note: two round O shapes make a pair of wheels

explanation.surface: A dry spike through the wheels means they need lubrication.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oil' sounds like the lubricant, but the answer is the perfume.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto, or attar, is a fragrant essential oil distilled from rose petals.

clue.text: Admiration for the posh truck carrying abnormal load (tons)

indicators.note: the lorry carries the other letters inside it
the letters of load are rearranged into an abnormal order

explanation.surface: A truck carries an abnormal load measured in tons.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the rare word for worship of the nobility; 'for the posh' completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lordolatry is the worship of lords, an excessive admiration for nobility and rank.

clue.text: Complaint of jet-setter, say, exposes Northern yokel with cape

parts.note: to air is to expose, so exposes is airs

indicators.note: speech in northern England is known for dropping the H

parts.note: a ness is a headland or cape

explanation.surface: An exposé of a northern country bumpkin with a cape.
explanation.walkthrough: Northern dialects drop the H, so HICK becomes ICK.
explanation.definitionFit: Airsickness is nausea caused by flying, a complaint for frequent travellers.

clue.text: Beverage near Parisian when getting in fuel

indicators.note: the French word gets inside the fuel brand

explanation.surface: A drink nearby while a Parisian refuels.
explanation.walkthrough: Esso is a well-known fuel brand.
explanation.definitionFit: Espresso is strong black coffee, a common drink.

clue.text: Couple of stewards on Irish loco describing lag?

parts.note: the first couple of letters of stewards

explanation.surface: Stewards aboard an Irish train are delayed.
explanation.walkthrough: A lag is an old lag, a convict; stir is prison slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Stir-crazy describes someone driven mad by long imprisonment, as a long-serving convict might be.

clue.text: Annoy macho sextet leaving

indicators.note: the six letters leave the word

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A macho group of six walks out.
explanation.walkthrough: VI, Roman six, leaves VIRILE.
explanation.definitionFit: To rile is to irritate or anger.

clue.text: Impressive flower up off the wall

indicators.note: off the wall means crazy, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A flower climbs up and off the garden wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Powerful means strong and forceful enough to impress.

clue.text: Rounded character following AC Milan occasionally cheers

indicators.note: the rounded character follows the Milan letters, so it is placed after them
occasionally means every other letter is taken

explanation.surface: AC Milan fans cheering occasionally after a rounded move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' puts O after the alternate letters of AC Milan.
explanation.definitionFit: Ciao is an informal Italian greeting or farewell, like the British cheers.

clue.text: Press newsman drinking whisky, at heart, was sarcastic

indicators.note: the press-and-newsman pair takes in, drinks, the other letters

parts.note: to press clothes is to iron

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letters

explanation.surface: A press journalist drinking whisky made a sardonic remark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' is the household verb, as with clothes, not the newspapers the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To ironise is to speak with irony, being sarcastic.

clue.text: Oops! My quiche is half covered in spirit

indicators.note: the front half of each word is covered over, hidden, so only the back half shows

explanation.surface: A cook exclaims that their quiche is half covered in alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: Cover the first half of each word: oo-PS, m-Y, qui-CHE.
explanation.definitionFit: The psyche is the soul or mind, the human spirit.

clue.text: Good book initially denied after means of payment no longer convenient

indicators.note: the book comes after the payment card

parts.note: Access was a British credit card, now defunct

indicators.note: the initial letter is denied

parts.note: the Good Book is the Bible

explanation.surface: A Bible bought on a card that is no longer handy.
explanation.walkthrough: Access was a UK credit card withdrawn in the 1990s, hence 'no longer'.
explanation.definitionFit: Accessible means easy to reach or use, so convenient.

clue.text: River in Rimini awkward to draw

indicators.note: draw spelt backwards is ward, so these letters are read from right to left
the letters are found within the words

explanation.surface: An artist in Rimini finds it awkward to draw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rimini' tempts as the river location; the letters lie within 'Rimini awkward', read right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kwai is a river in Thailand, famous from the film The Bridge on the River Kwai.

clue.text: Insurance company poaches the French assistant virtually

indicators.note: the insurer takes in, poaches, the French article

parts.note: AXA is a French insurance company

explanation.surface: An insurance company poaches staff from France.
explanation.walkthrough: AXA is a large insurer.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexa is Amazon's voice-controlled virtual assistant.

clue.text: Out of uniform, cowboy pockets unknown secretary's fare in Spain

indicators.note: the cowboy pockets, holds inside, the other letters
a cowboy out of uniform has taken it off, so that letter is removed from his name

parts.note: a gaucho is a South American cowboy
U is uniform in the NATO alphabet
a PA, personal assistant, is a secretary

explanation.surface: A cowboy out of uniform pockets a secretary's fare during a Spanish trip.
explanation.walkthrough: GAUCHO loses U to give GACHO, which takes in Z and PA.
explanation.definitionFit: Gazpacho is a chilled Spanish tomato soup.

clue.text: Spin disc, supporting

explanation.surface: A DJ spins a disc for supporters.
explanation.definitionFit: Pro means in favour of, as opposed to anti.

clue.text: Exercised calf perhaps left by river in periphery of field

indicators.note: the left-and-river letters go in between the outer letters
the periphery of a word is its edge, its first and last letters

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon

explanation.surface: A calf exercised by a river at the edge of a field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calf' looks like a young cow in the field, but it is a muscle.
explanation.definitionFit: A muscle such as a calf is flexed when tensed or worked.

clue.text: Type of bed obtained fills the ancient cell

parts.note: a Z-bed is a folding bed

indicators.note: the word for obtained fills the old article

explanation.surface: A bed obtained for an ancient prison cell.
explanation.walkthrough: A Z-bed is a folding bed, so the type is Z.
explanation.definitionFit: A zygote is the fertilised egg cell formed when two gametes unite.

clue.text: Duty of Yankee with musical instrument to keep amp in case

indicators.note: the instrument keeps the other letters inside

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for ampere

explanation.surface: A sax player is told to keep the amplifier in its case.
explanation.walkthrough: Yankee here means American; sales tax is the US name for a levy on purchases.
explanation.definitionFit: Sales tax is an American levy on goods, the US counterpart of VAT.
